topics.title: F.1 Values, owners, and borrows
topics.summary: Value semantics. An object behaves as a meaningful value under its documented copying, comparison, and mutation rules. Independent value copies are a design goal for many domain types, but shared or borrowed members can change those semantics. Ask whether modifying one copy can affect another through an alias.

blocks.text: Value semantics. An object behaves as a meaningful value under its documented copying, comparison, and mutation rules. Independent value copies are a design goal for many domain types, but shared or borrowed members can change those semantics. Ask whether modifying one copy can affect another through an alias.

blocks.text: Owner. The object or subsystem responsible for a resource’s lifetime. Ownership includes responsibility for release, not merely permission to access. Ask which exact destructor or explicit completion path ends that responsibility and whether another object can accidentally release the same resource.
rich: The object or subsystem responsible for a resource’s lifetime. Ownership includes responsibility for release, not merely permission to access. Ask which exact destructor or explicit completion path ends that responsibility and whether another object can accidentally release the same resource.

blocks.text: Borrow. Temporary access to an object owned elsewhere, commonly represented by a reference, pointer, iterator, span, or string view. Ask what must remain alive and unchanged during use, and whether the borrow escapes the scope in which those facts are established.
rich: Temporary access to an object owned elsewhere, commonly represented by a reference, pointer, iterator, span, or string view. Ask what must remain alive and unchanged during use, and whether the borrow escapes the scope in which those facts are established.

blocks.text: RAII. Associate resource responsibility with an object’s lifetime so cleanup occurs when that lifetime ends. Ask separately how acquisition failure, successful completion, and fallback cleanup are reported. RAII does not itself reverse external side effects or restore a previously modified domain value.
rich: Associate resource responsibility with an object’s lifetime so cleanup occurs when that lifetime ends. Ask separately how acquisition failure, successful completion, and fallback cleanup are reported. RAII does not itself reverse external side effects or restore a previously modified domain value.

blocks.text: Rule of Zero. Use members with correct ownership behavior so the containing type does not need unnecessary custom copy, move, or destruction machinery. Ask whether memberwise operations also preserve relationships between members, such as a cached size and the storage it describes.
rich: Use members with correct ownership behavior so the containing type does not need unnecessary custom copy, move, or destruction machinery. Ask whether memberwise operations also preserve relationships between members, such as a cached size and the storage it describes.

blocks.text: Moved-from state. The state left after a move operation has been applied. Its permitted uses come from the type’s contract. Ask whether the type promises emptiness, a valid unspecified value, or another explicit state; do not assume that every move sets a source to zero.

blocks.text: Aliasing shared ownership. A shared owner exposes one pointer while retaining the ownership group of another object, such as an enclosing snapshot. Ask whether the exposed subobject remains valid for the owner’s lifetime and whether later mutation can invalidate that relationship.

topics.title: F.2 Interfaces and guarantees
topics.summary: Class invariant. A relationship that valid observable states of a class must satisfy. Ask which operations can change the relevant members and where validation occurs before those changes become public. A comment saying “valid range” is weaker than an interface that prevents invalid mutation.

blocks.text: Class invariant. A relationship that valid observable states of a class must satisfy. Ask which operations can change the relevant members and where validation occurs before those changes become public. A comment saying “valid range” is weaker than an interface that prevents invalid mutation.
rich: A relationship that valid observable states of a class must satisfy. Ask which operations can change the relevant members and where validation occurs before those changes become public. A comment saying “valid range” is weaker than an interface that prevents invalid mutation.

blocks.text: Strong exception guarantee. Failure preserves the specified observable state. Ask where that state boundary ends: input positions, diagnostics, counters, and remote effects can lie outside it. A guarantee without a named boundary is easy to overstate.
rich: Failure preserves the specified observable state. Ask where that state boundary ends: input positions, diagnostics, counters, and remote effects can lie outside it. A guarantee without a named boundary is easy to overstate.

blocks.text: Commit point. The operation at which a validated candidate replaces accepted state. Ask which earlier steps can fail, whether publication itself can fail, and which object cleans up the old state after success. A visible commit point simplifies both review and testing.
rich: The operation at which a validated candidate replaces accepted state. Ask which earlier steps can fail, whether publication itself can fail, and which object cleans up the old state after success. A visible commit point simplifies both review and testing.

blocks.text: Runtime polymorphism. Dispatch behavior through a common interface to the active dynamic implementation. Ask whether base destruction is safe, overrides match the intended signatures, and derived behavior respects the interface’s semantic contract rather than only its function types.
rich: Dispatch behavior through a common interface to the active dynamic implementation. Ask whether base destruction is safe, overrides match the intended signatures, and derived behavior respects the interface’s semantic contract rather than only its function types.

blocks.text: Composition. Build behavior from smaller components with explicit ownership or borrowing relationships. Ask whether copying the composed object copies its dependencies or shares access to them. A reference member can make two apparent value copies write through the same external sink.
rich: Build behavior from smaller components with explicit ownership or borrowing relationships. Ask whether copying the composed object copies its dependencies or shares access to them. A reference member can make two apparent value copies write through the same external sink.

blocks.text: Concept. A named compile-time constraint on template arguments or expressions. Ask which semantic laws remain outside syntactic checking. A comparator can satisfy invocation requirements while violating ordering laws; an integer type can satisfy a concept while particular values overflow.

topics.title: F.3 Traversal, algorithms, and result models
topics.summary: Iterator invalidation. A change that makes a previously obtained iterator unusable under the relevant container or range rules. Ask about cached end iterators as well as element iterators, and distinguish iterator stability from the stability of an element’s logical identity.

blocks.text: Projection. A function selecting the part of an element used by a range algorithm. Ask whether the projected value owns its data or borrows it and whether comparison over the projected domain satisfies the algorithm’s requirements.
rich: A function selecting the part of an element used by a range algorithm. Ask whether the projected value owns its data or borrows it and whether comparison over the projected domain satisfies the algorithm’s requirements.
blocks.headingContext: F.3 Traversal, algorithms, and result models

blocks.text: Strict weak ordering. The semantic ordering relationship required by many sorting and ordered-container operations. Ask about self-comparison, contradictory directions, transitivity, and equivalence groups. A comparator using less-than-or-equal is not a valid substitute for strict precedence.
rich: The semantic ordering relationship required by many sorting and ordered-container operations. Ask about self-comparison, contradictory directions, transitivity, and equivalence groups. A comparator using less-than-or-equal is not a valid substitute for strict precedence.
blocks.headingContext: F.3 Traversal, algorithms, and result models

blocks.text: Stable sorting. Preserve prior relative order among comparator-equivalent elements. Ask whether prior order is itself stable across runs. If output must be independent of arrival order, define explicit tie-break keys instead of relying on stability alone.
rich: Preserve prior relative order among comparator-equivalent elements. Ask whether prior order is itself stable across runs. If output must be independent of arrival order, define explicit tie-break keys instead of relying on stability alone.
blocks.headingContext: F.3 Traversal, algorithms, and result models

blocks.text: View. A range representation intended for efficient manipulation under its specific ownership and complexity rules. Ask what it owns, what it borrows, what state it caches, and when computations occur. Do not assume that every view is non-owning or that every pipeline materializes data.
rich: A range representation intended for efficient manipulation under its specific ownership and complexity rules. Ask what it owns, what it borrows, what state it caches, and when computations occur. Do not assume that every view is non-owning or that every pipeline materializes data.
blocks.headingContext: F.3 Traversal, algorithms, and result models

blocks.text: Materialization. Construct an owning collection or result from a traversal recipe. Ask whether the allocation and copying buy a needed independent lifetime, stable value, or effect boundary. Avoiding materialization is not inherently better when callers must retain the result.
rich: Construct an owning collection or result from a traversal recipe. Ask whether the allocation and copying buy a needed independent lifetime, stable value, or effect boundary. Avoiding materialization is not inherently better when callers must retain the result.
blocks.headingContext: F.3 Traversal, algorithms, and result models

blocks.text: Optional. An engaged value or absence of that value. Ask what absence means and whether a fallback would erase an important distinction. An optional string view still borrows bytes; the wrapper owns only the view object.
rich: An engaged value or absence of that value. Ask what absence means and whether a fallback would erase an important distinction. An optional string view still borrows bytes; the wrapper owns only the view object.
blocks.headingContext: F.3 Traversal, algorithms, and result models

blocks.text: Variant. One active alternative from a closed set of types, with documented exceptional-state behavior. Ask whether every alternative has a meaningful handler and whether default construction chooses the state the domain actually intends.

topics.title: F.4 External operations and evidence
topics.summary: Completion. The point at which an operation’s required result has been checked, distinct from eventual destructor cleanup. Ask whether final output, flush, or close failures are observed before success is reported. Ordinary completion is not automatically crash durability.

blocks.text: Completion. The point at which an operation’s required result has been checked, distinct from eventual destructor cleanup. Ask whether final output, flush, or close failures are observed before success is reported. Ordinary completion is not automatically crash durability.
rich: The point at which an operation’s required result has been checked, distinct from eventual destructor cleanup. Ask whether final output, flush, or close failures are observed before success is reported. Ordinary completion is not automatically crash durability.

blocks.text: Deterministic fixture. A saved input and expected contract whose result can be compared directly. Ask whether the expectation is hand-derived or independent of the implementation under test. A seed alone may not reproduce a library distribution’s exact generated sequence across implementations.
rich: A saved input and expected contract whose result can be compared directly. Ask whether the expectation is hand-derived or independent of the implementation under test. A seed alone may not reproduce a library distribution’s exact generated sequence across implementations.

blocks.text: Verification boundary. The scope supported by actual executed checks. Ask which compilers, standard libraries, platforms, configurations, and cases were tested. A precise limitation makes evidence more useful; it does not erase the value of the checks that genuinely passed.
